newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans reparations for nationalised hotels.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans reparations for nationalised hotels.

text.p: Romania's centrist government is working on a law to award reparations to hotel owners stripped of their properties by the ousted communists, Tourism Minister Akos Birtalan said.

In a weekend interview, Birtalan said a law on reparations for nationalised hotels, due for completion when parliament returns from summer recess in September, was being drafted by the tourism and justice ministries.
"The government cannot fulfil its pledges to privatise tourist assets quickly without settling reparations due to former owners," Birtalan said.

"There are around 1,000 hotels, villas and chalets still owned by the state. Some might be returned to their former owners, should they wish to claim them back. Unfortunately, full-scale return is no longer possible."

Unlike more advanced East Europeans Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic, post-communist Romania had failed to address the issue of compensation for hotels, banks or industries seized by the communists after World War Two.
A 1991 law turned communist-era companies into shareholding ventures ready for privatisation, but no legislation has been drawn up since on compensating their pre-war owners.

Dozens of villas and hotels across the Balkan country have already been delivered into private hands by the leftist administration defeated in last year's elections. A legal ruling on compensation was left in abeyance.

Birtalan said reparation plans involved giving cash compensation or shares in companies from the portfolio held by the main government agency in charge of privatisation, the State Ownership Fund. He did not elaborate.
Tourism in Romania suffers from lack of infrastructure, bad roads and communications and poor or surly service.
Birtalan said he hoped to complete privatisation of the sector by the end of the year to bring standards up to those in Western countries.

"Romania has huge tourism resources, but its tourism potential is not up to the mark," he said. Earnings from tourism accounted for less than three percent of gross domestic product in the post-communist era.
Birtalan is one of two cabinet members representing Romania's 1.6 million-strong ethnic Hungarian minority. The coalition groups Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and Liberals.
